topics.title: What parties are and what they do

learn.hook: Imagine an election with 500 independent candidates and no parties. Who would form the government? Who would be responsible? Parties solve this puzzle.
points: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government. They agree on some policies and programmes for society, aiming at the collective good.
A party has three components: leaders, active members, and followers (supporters). Since a party is a part of society, it involves partisanship — taking a side on issues.

Functions of parties: (1) contest elections — in most democracies candidates are put up by parties; (2) put forward different policies and programmes for voters to choose from; (3) play a decisive role in making laws; (4) form and run governments; (5) those that lose play the role of opposition, criticising the government and mobilising people.

(6) Shape public opinion by raising and highlighting issues; (7) provide people access to government machinery and welfare schemes — local party leaders are easier to approach than government officers.

Why we need parties: without them every candidate would be independent, no one could promise major policy changes, and no one would be responsible for running the country. Parties grew along with representative democracies.

example.q: Think it through: In the USA, members and supporters of a party choose its candidates. How is this different in India?
steps: In some countries, such as the USA, party members and supporters select candidates.
In India, top party leaders usually choose the candidates.
Both are ways of carrying out the first function of parties — contesting elections.
example.answer: In India top party leaders choose the candidates, while in the USA members and supporters do.

learn.reallife: Before elections, parties release manifestos listing their promises on jobs, farming, schools and health — that is the 'policies and programmes' function at work.

games.title: Match the function of parties
pairs: Put up candidates for voters to choose
Criticise the government and voice different views

games.title: True or false: political parties
items: A political party has three components: leaders, active members and followers.
These three together make up a party.
In India, candidates of a party are usually chosen by top party leaders.
In the USA, members and supporters choose candidates.
Parties that lose elections have no role until the next election.
They act as the opposition, criticising and checking the government.
Without parties, every candidate would be independent and no one would be responsible for running the country.
This is why parties are needed in representative democracy.
Partisanship means a party never takes sides on any issue.
Partisanship means taking a side and being inclined towards a particular view.

quiz.q: What is a political party?
options: A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government
A group that runs only charities
quiz.explain: Parties seek to win elections and hold power so that they can carry out their policies.
quiz.mistake: Confuses parties with government bodies or charities

quiz.q: Which are the three components of a political party?
quiz.explain: Every party has leaders, active members and followers or supporters.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up a party's structure with government posts

quiz.q: What role do parties that lose an election play in a democracy?
options: They act as the opposition and criticise the government
quiz.explain: The opposition voices different views, criticises the government for its failures and mobilises people.
quiz.mistake: Thinks losing parties have no role between elections

quiz.q: Who usually chooses a party's candidates in India?
quiz.explain: In India top party leaders generally choose candidates; in the USA party members and supporters do.
quiz.mistake: Confuses India's practice with the USA's

quiz.q: How do parties shape public opinion?
options: By raising and highlighting issues and launching movements
quiz.explain: Parties raise issues, and their members and supporters spread their views across society.
quiz.mistake: Does not see parties as a link between people and issues

quiz.q: Why is it often easier for a citizen to approach a local party leader than a government officer?
options: Party leaders have the power to make laws alone
Party leaders need people's support and votes, so they listen to them
Officers are banned from meeting people
quiz.explain: Leaders depend on public support, so they try to help people reach government machinery and welfare schemes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks party leaders hold official power over officers

quiz.q: What would most likely happen in a democracy without political parties?
options: Every candidate would be independent, and no one would be responsible for running the country
The courts would choose the government
quiz.explain: Without parties, no one could promise major policy changes or take collective responsibility.
quiz.mistake: Assumes democracy would work the same without parties

quiz.q: What does 'partisanship' mean?
options: Taking a side and being inclined towards a particular view
quiz.explain: A party is a 'part' of society, so it takes sides; this is partisanship.
quiz.mistake: Confuses partisanship with neutrality

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do we even need political parties? What jobs do they do?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Parties contest elections, offer policies, form governments or opposition — democracy needs them!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you name a few functions, like contesting elections or acting as opposition?

topics.title: Party systems: one, two or many

learn.hook: Some countries are like a one-team match, some like India vs Australia, and some like the IPL with many teams. Which party system fits where?
points: One-party system: only one party is allowed to control and run the government. In China, only the Communist Party is allowed to rule. This is not a democratic option, because voters have no real choice.
Two-party system: power usually changes between two main parties. Other parties exist but rarely win enough seats. The United States of America and the United Kingdom are examples.
Multiparty system: several parties compete for power, and more than two have a reasonable chance of coming to power, either on their own or in alliance. India has a multiparty system.

When several parties come together to contest elections and win power, the group is called an alliance or a front. A multiparty system can look messy and may lead to political instability, but it allows a variety of interests and opinions to be represented.

No party system is ideal for all countries. A party system is not chosen by a country; it evolves over a long time depending on the nature of society, its social and regional divisions, its history and its system of elections.

example.q: Think it through: Why has India ended up with a multiparty system rather than a two-party system?
steps: India is very large and has great social and geographical diversity.
Different regions and groups have their own concerns and want them represented.
Two parties cannot easily absorb all this diversity, so many parties emerged.
example.answer: Because India's size and social and regional diversity are better reflected by many parties.

learn.reallife: During elections you see many party symbols on the EVM — from national parties to state parties — a living picture of India's multiparty system.

quiz.q: Which country has a one-party system?
quiz.explain: In China only the Communist Party is allowed to rule.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any large country has a one-party system

quiz.q: Why is a one-party system not considered a good democratic option?
options: Voters do not get a real choice
quiz.explain: Democracy needs at least two parties competing so that voters can choose.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fewer parties means better democracy

quiz.q: Which pair of countries are examples of a two-party system?
options: United States of America and United Kingdom
India and United States of America
quiz.explain: In the USA and the UK, power usually changes between two main parties.
quiz.mistake: Places India or China in the two-party category

quiz.q: India's party system is best described as:
quiz.explain: Several parties in India compete, and more than two have a reasonable chance of coming to power.
quiz.mistake: Notices two big parties and forgets the many others

quiz.q: What is an alliance or front?
options: When several parties come together to contest elections and win power
When a party splits into two
When one party bans the others
quiz.explain: In a multiparty system, parties often join hands as an alliance or front.
quiz.mistake: Confuses an alliance with a party split

quiz.q: What is one advantage of a multiparty system?
options: It allows a variety of interests and opinions to enjoy political representation
It always gives a stable government
quiz.explain: Many parties can represent many groups and views, though it may sometimes cause instability.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a multiparty system guarantees stability

quiz.q: How does a country get its party system?
options: It is chosen by the President
It is copied from another country
It evolves over a long time based on the society, its divisions, history and election system
It is fixed by the Supreme Court
quiz.explain: Party systems are not chosen; they develop from a country's society and history.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a country can simply choose its party system

quiz.q: In a two-party system, what usually happens?
options: Power usually changes between two main parties, though other parties may exist
Many parties regularly form coalition governments
quiz.explain: Other parties exist, but the two main parties usually win enough seats to form the government by turn.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only two parties are legally allowed in a two-party system

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'One party, two parties, many parties — what's the difference? Explain with examples!'
teach.praise: Chirp! China one, USA and UK two, India many — and alliances help in a multiparty world!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you give an example of each system and say what an alliance is?

learn.hook: Every party symbol on the ballot has a story. Which parties get a fixed symbol, and how do they become national or state parties?
points: Every party in India has to register with the Election Commission. The Commission treats all parties equally but gives some special facilities to large, established parties.
Parties given these facilities are called 'recognised' parties. A recognised party gets a unique election symbol, which only its official candidates can use.
State party (as per the textbook): a party that secures at least 6% of the total votes in an election to the Legislative Assembly of a state and wins at least two seats.

National party (as per the textbook): a party that secures at least 6% of the total votes in Lok Sabha elections or in Assembly elections in four states, and wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha.

State parties are often called 'regional parties', but they need not be regional in ideology. Over time, state parties have become stronger, and since 1996 nearly every state party has had a chance to be part of a national-level coalition government, strengthening federalism.

example.q: Think it through: Party P gets 7% of the votes in a state Assembly election and wins three seats. Does it qualify as a state party?
steps: The textbook rule needs at least 6% of the total votes in the Assembly election.
It also needs at least two seats.
7% is more than 6%, and three seats are more than two.
example.answer: Yes. Party P meets both conditions, so it can be recognised as a state party.

learn.reallife: Look at the ballot paper or EVM list in your area: recognised parties appear with their fixed symbols, while many independents get symbols from a free list.

quiz.q: With which body must every political party in India register?
quiz.explain: All parties have to register with the Election Commission.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Election Commission with other institutions

quiz.q: What special facility does a recognised party get?
options: A unique election symbol that only its official candidates can use
The right to rule without elections
quiz.explain: Recognised parties get a fixed symbol that only their official candidates may use.
quiz.mistake: Thinks recognition gives power without elections

quiz.q: According to the textbook, what minimum share of votes in a state Assembly election does a party need, along with at least two seats, to be a state party?
quiz.explain: A state party needs at least 6% of total votes in the Assembly election and at least two seats.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the number of seats with the vote percentage

quiz.q: To be a national party (as per the textbook), how many Lok Sabha seats must a party win along with the vote condition?
quiz.explain: A national party needs at least 6% of votes in Lok Sabha or in Assembly elections in four states, and at least four Lok Sabha seats.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the seat requirement with the 6% vote share

quiz.q: Party Q wins 8% of the votes in a state Assembly election but only one seat. Can it be recognised as a state party under the textbook rule?
options: No, because it won fewer than two seats
Yes, because it crossed 6% of votes
Yes, because it won at least one seat
No, because it needs 10% of votes
quiz.explain: Both conditions must be met: at least 6% votes and at least two seats. One seat is not enough.
quiz.mistake: Checks only the vote share and forgets the seat condition

quiz.q: Why are state parties sometimes called 'regional parties'?
options: Because they are banned from national politics
Because they are recognised on the basis of their strength in a state
Because they are run by the Central government
quiz.explain: Their recognition depends on performance in a state, though their ideas need not be regional.
quiz.mistake: Thinks state parties cannot take part in national politics

quiz.q: How has the growing strength of state parties affected Indian democracy?
options: It has ended elections to the Lok Sabha
It has made state parties part of national coalition governments, strengthening federalism
It has made India a one-party system
quiz.explain: Since 1996 nearly every state party has had a chance to be part of a national-level coalition government.
quiz.mistake: Thinks state parties matter only within their state

quiz.q: A party wins 6% of the votes in Assembly elections in four states and also wins four Lok Sabha seats. As per the textbook rule, it qualifies as a:
options: Registered party only, with no recognition
quiz.explain: It meets both national party conditions: at least 6% votes in Assembly elections in four states and at least four Lok Sabha seats.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Assembly votes can count only towards state party status

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a party become a national party or a state party? What do they get?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Register with the Election Commission, win enough votes and seats, and get recognised with a symbol!
teach.nudge: Good! What percentage of votes and how many seats does the textbook rule need for each kind of party?

topics.title: Challenges to parties and how to reform them

learn.hook: Parties are the engine of democracy — but even a great engine needs servicing. What goes wrong, and how can we fix it?
points: Challenge 1 — lack of internal democracy: power gets concentrated in a few top leaders; parties do not keep membership registers, hold organisational meetings or conduct internal elections regularly.

Challenge 2 — dynastic succession: top positions often go to members of one family, which is unfair to other members. Challenge 3 — growing role of money and muscle power, especially during elections. Challenge 4 — lack of meaningful choice, as differences in the policies of parties have reduced.

Reforms already made: the Constitution was amended to stop elected MLAs and MPs from changing parties (anti-defection law) — a member who changes party loses the seat. The Supreme Court made it mandatory for every candidate to file an affidavit giving details of property and pending criminal cases. The Election Commission made it necessary for parties to hold organisational elections and file income tax returns.

Suggested reforms: a law to regulate the internal affairs of parties; making it compulsory to give about one-third of tickets to women candidates; and state funding of elections, where the government gives parties money to support their election expenses.
Pressure from citizens matters too: people can press parties through petitions, publicity and agitations, and those who want reform can themselves join political parties.

example.q: Think it through: How does a candidate's affidavit help voters?
steps: The affidavit lists the candidate's property and any criminal cases pending against them.
This information is made public before voting.
Voters can use it to make a more informed choice.
example.answer: It gives voters information about a candidate's assets and criminal cases so they can choose wisely.

learn.reallife: Before elections, news channels and websites often publish summaries of candidates' affidavits — that is this reform in action.

quiz.q: What is meant by 'lack of internal democracy' in a party?
options: Power is concentrated in a few leaders, and the party does not hold regular internal elections or meetings
The party contests too many elections
The party has too many ordinary members
The party follows the law strictly
quiz.explain: Without internal democracy, ordinary members have little say in decisions.
quiz.mistake: Confuses internal democracy with elections to the legislature

quiz.q: What is 'dynastic succession'?
options: Top positions going to members of one family
quiz.explain: In dynastic succession, family members of leaders get top posts, which is unfair to other members.
quiz.mistake: Confuses dynastic succession with defection

quiz.q: What does the anti-defection law do?
options: It bans parties from contesting elections
It allows MLAs to switch parties freely
An elected MLA or MP who changes party loses the seat
quiz.explain: The Constitution was amended so that legislators who change parties lose their seat in the legislature.
quiz.mistake: Thinks defection is encouraged by the law

quiz.q: Which body ordered that candidates must file an affidavit giving details of their property and criminal cases?
quiz.explain: The Supreme Court passed this order to reduce the influence of money and criminals in elections.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the affidavit order with the Election Commission's order

quiz.q: Which body made it necessary for parties to hold organisational elections and file income tax returns?
quiz.explain: This was an order of the Election Commission.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Supreme Court's affidavit order

quiz.q: What is 'state funding of elections'?
options: The government gives parties money to support their election expenses
quiz.explain: It is a suggested reform to reduce the influence of money in elections.
quiz.mistake: Thinks state funding means paying voters

quiz.q: Which of these is a suggested reform, not one already made?
options: A law making it compulsory to give about one-third of tickets to women candidates
Organisational elections ordered by the Election Commission
quiz.explain: Giving about one-third of party tickets to women is a suggestion; the others have already been put in place. (The 2023 women's reservation amendment reserves seats in legislatures; it does not make parties give tickets to women.)
quiz.mistake: Does not separate reforms already made from suggestions

quiz.q: Which challenge refers to the reduced differences in policies among major parties?
quiz.explain: When parties' policies look alike, voters do not get a meaningful choice.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the four challenges

teach.ask: Gappu peeps: 'What problems do political parties face, and how can we make them better?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Name the problems, then fix them with laws, court orders, Election Commission rules and people's pressure!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you name two challenges and two reforms, like the anti-defection law or affidavits?
